paragraphs: A probabilistic model needs to describe both ordinary outcomes and the rare extremes in its distribution's tails. Models that transform noise through neural networks can misrepresent these extremes when the starting noise distribution has unsuitable tails. This paper develops a systematic way to track tail behavior through the operations that define a probabilistic model.

The method represents tail behavior using a three-parameter family based on the generalized Gamma distribution. Its algebra describes how these representations change when random variables are added or multiplied, with results remaining inside the same family. It also distinguishes sub-Gaussian tails with different scales and handles ratios well enough to recover the tails of many important statistical distributions from their definitions.

The authors show how a probabilistic programming compiler could apply this analysis before drawing samples. That makes tail information available when preparing inference, rather than relying entirely on sampled outcomes to reveal extreme behavior. Experiments report improved performance on several density modeling and variational inference tasks when inference algorithms use the proposed algebra.
neurips-2023-a-heavy-tailed-algebra-for-.tldr: A mathematical algebra tracks distribution tails through probabilistic programs and improves inference in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: In transductive online learning, a learner knows the full sequence of inputs before making predictions, but must still predict their labels through an online interaction. The adversary fixes those inputs at the start. This paper asks how many mistakes a learner must make in this setting and how that number changes as the sequence becomes longer.

The main result establishes exactly three possible growth patterns for the optimal mistake count: n, logarithmic in n, or bounded by a constant as n grows. Which pattern occurs depends on a combination of VC dimension and Littlestone dimension. These mathematical measures therefore help determine whether advance knowledge of the inputs permits a bounded, slowly growing, or fully linear mistake count.

The paper also provides quantitative upper and lower bounds using combinatorial dimensions. In the constant-growth case, it strengthens a known lower bound from the square root of log d to log d, where d is the Littlestone dimension. Here, constant means independent of sequence length, not independent of the learning problem. Extensions cover multiclass classification and the agnostic setting.
neurips-2023-a-trichotomy-for-transducti.tldr: Optimal mistake counts in transductive online learning fall into exactly three growth regimes determined by combinatorial dimensions.

paragraphs: Image editing can require selecting a piece of an object, an entire entity, or two entities connected by a meaningful relationship. Accurate segmentation at one of these levels does not cover all those selection needs. This paper introduces All-Inclusive Multi-Level Segmentation, or AIMS, as a task that explicitly brings the three levels together.

The authors build one model through training across multiple datasets and tasks. This creates two central challenges: annotations from different sources can be inconsistent, and the segmentation tasks have relationships that the model should account for. The proposed design includes task complementarity, task association, and a prompt mask encoder to support predictions at the part, entity, and relation levels.

The contribution makes the level of selection an explicit part of the segmentation problem. A relation-level region, in particular, concerns two semantically related entities rather than only one isolated entity. Experiments report effective segmentation and generalization compared with leading methods developed on individual datasets and concurrent segment-anything work. These findings support the usefulness of training a unified model for several kinds of editing selection.
neurips-2023-aims-all-inclusive-multi-le.tldr: AIMS combines part, entity, and relationship segmentation in one model to support varied image-editing selections.

paragraphs: Alexa Arena is a simulation platform for studying assistive agents that combine conversation with actions in an environment. Its focus is the interaction between people and embodied agents: users can participate in tasks involving a simulated world, while researchers develop and evaluate systems intended to help them complete those tasks.

The environment provides layouts containing multiple rooms and many objects that can be interacted with. User-friendly graphics and controls support robotic tasks presented in a game-like form. Making those tasks accessible to general users is central to the platform's purpose, because human participation supplies data for research and enables evaluation of how an embodied system performs during interaction.

Alongside the simulator, the authors introduce a task-completion benchmark that includes dialogue and online human evaluation. This pairs a place to build interactive tasks with a way to assess agents completing them with people. The stated contribution is research infrastructure for efficient data collection and evaluation, with conversation and environmental interaction brought together in the same platform.
neurips-2023-alexa-arena-a-user-centric-.tldr: Alexa Arena provides an accessible simulator and human-evaluated benchmark for conversational agents that act in interactive environments.

paragraphs: Generalized additive models express a prediction as a sum of separate, potentially nonlinear feature contributions. That structure makes them appealing for interpretation because each contribution can be examined individually. However, dependencies between features can create concurvity: different contribution curves can compensate for one another, making the apparent explanation ambiguous even when the combined prediction remains useful.

This paper shows how seriously that ambiguity can undermine interpretation and proposes a regularizer to reduce it. The regularizer penalizes pairwise correlations between the transformed feature variables that enter the additive prediction. It therefore targets dependence in the learned contributions, including dependence arising through nonlinear transformations, rather than considering only relationships between the original input values.

The approach applies to differentiable additive models, including Neural Additive Models and NeuralProphet. Experiments use synthetic and real-world tabular and time-series data. They show that the regularizer can reduce concurvity without significantly sacrificing prediction quality, while also reducing variation in feature importance. The practical benefit is a clearer allocation of contributions among features, with less ambiguity from contributions that cancel each other.
neurips-2023-curve-your-enthusiasm-concu.tldr: Penalizing correlations between learned feature contributions makes additive models more interpretable without significantly reducing predictive quality in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks are attractive because they can combine low energy requirements with accuracy comparable to conventional neural networks. Training them is difficult because the step function that produces spikes does not provide the gradient information ordinary training relies on. A common workaround uses the actual spike function for prediction and a differentiable substitute when propagating training signals backward.

This paper proposes applying a zeroth-order technique locally, at the level of individual neurons. The motivation includes regularizing effects and the possibility of more energy-efficient training. The authors also establish a theoretical connection to existing surrogate-gradient methods, helping relate the proposed training approach to the workaround already used for spiking networks.

Experiments cover both static image datasets and neuromorphic datasets, including CIFAR, ImageNet-100, and event-based recognition tasks. The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art results in their evaluation. They also describe compatibility with efficient backpropagation implementations that could yield an overall training speedup of three to four times. That speedup is presented as a possibility enabled by implementation, while the energy benefit is likewise a motivation rather than a quantified finding.
neurips-2023-direct-training-of-snn-usin.tldr: Neuron-level zeroth-order training improves reported spiking-network results and could support faster, more energy-efficient implementations.

paragraphs: Open-world semi-supervised learning uses a partially labeled set of known classes to classify unlabeled examples that may also belong to new classes. The paper argues that treating labels at only one level overlooks useful structure. Examples can share relationships at narrower subclass levels and broader superclass levels, even when their target classes differ or are unknown.

The proposed TIDA framework discovers and connects these levels. One module constructs hierarchical prototypes in the learned representation space, providing reference points for subclass, target-class, and superclass concepts. A second module aligns predictions across the hierarchy so that predictions at different levels remain consistent. Those relationships provide additional supervision for learning representations and producing pseudo labels for unlabeled examples.

The authors explain the mutual benefit of discovery and alignment through the expectation-maximization perspective. Experiments on seven commonly used datasets report significant improvements and new state-of-the-art performance. The findings support using relationships across multiple levels of meaning to improve recognition of both known and novel classes, instead of relying entirely on a single set of class boundaries.
neurips-2023-discover-and-align-taxonomi.tldr: TIDA discovers hierarchical class relationships and aligns predictions across them to improve open-world semi-supervised recognition.

paragraphs: Adaptive experiments update treatment-assignment probabilities as evidence accumulates. This can use data more efficiently than fixed randomization, but it also means participant groups may receive very different chances of treatment. The paper addresses that tension while recognizing that groups expected to benefit greatly from treatment may appropriately receive it more often.

The proposed strategy combines efficient data use, an envy-free treatment-assignment guarantee, and improved overall participant welfare. It does not require parametric models for outcome variables. This matters because the allocation strategy can be studied without first committing to a particular parametric description of how participant outcomes are distributed.

The theoretical analysis characterizes convergence rates for group-level treatment-effect estimates and their associated standard deviations. It also proves that the assignment algorithm approaches the optimal allocation rule asymptotically, despite lacking a closed-form expression. The proof accounts for decisions depending on previously collected data, a dependence that complicates statistical inference. Simulations and two synthetic-data studies illustrate the strategy's performance alongside these guarantees.
neurips-2023-fair-adaptive-experiments-5.tldr: A fair adaptive experiment strategy balances estimation efficiency, an envy-free assignment guarantee, and participant welfare.

paragraphs: Differentially private model training usually applies one privacy budget across the training data. That budget expresses the allowed privacy loss, but people may have different preferences about that allowance. A shared setting can therefore be more restrictive than some contributors want while failing to provide the level of protection others expect.

This paper introduces individualized privacy budgets and a training procedure that supports them. The method, Individualized DP-SGD, adapts the standard differentially private stochastic gradient descent algorithm. It changes both how training data are sampled and how noise is added to gradients, allowing privacy guarantees to reflect the preferences associated with individual users and their data points.

The authors empirically find improved privacy-utility trade-offs with this approach. The significance is that privacy preferences become part of the training design, rather than being compressed into a single common budget. The reported improvement concerns the balance between useful model behavior and tailored protection; it does not require every contributor to accept the same privacy allowance.
neurips-2023-have-it-your-way-individual.tldr: Individualized DP-SGD adapts sampling and gradient noise to support different privacy budgets and empirically improve privacy-utility trade-offs.

paragraphs: An agent interacting with multiple objects may encounter new combinations, unfamiliar object properties, or tasks assembled from previously learned tasks. Representing each object separately helps, but the authors argue that further structure is available within objects themselves. DAFT-RL learns how individual object attributes contribute to dynamics, rewards, and interactions.

The framework extracts objects from visual inputs, assigns them to classes, and infers their latent parameters. For each class, a template graph describes how dynamics and rewards factor across attributes. Another graph describes attribute-level interactions between object classes. A dynamic interaction graph then represents the interactions among the objects present in a particular environment.

Together, these structures support a policy that can be applied in a new environment by estimating its interactions and latent parameters. This connects reusable class-level knowledge to the particular objects currently encountered. Evaluation on three benchmark datasets reports better generalization than state-of-the-art methods for unseen objects with varying attributes and latent parameters, as well as for tasks composed from previously learned tasks.
neurips-2023-learning-dynamic-attribute-.tldr: DAFT-RL models object attributes and their interactions to improve generalization to unfamiliar objects and composed tasks.

paragraphs: Prompts let a language model perform many tasks, but long instructions consume context space and cost computation each time they are encoded. Specializing a model through training can remove repeated prompting, yet typically requires separate retraining for each task. This paper introduces gisting as a way to retain reusable prompt information in a much smaller representation.

A gist model learns to compress a prompt into a small set of gist tokens that can be cached and reused. Training changes the Transformer's attention masks to encourage information to pass through this compressed representation. The authors state that this can be incorporated without additional cost beyond standard instruction finetuning, making compression part of the existing training process.

Experiments use both a decoder model, LLaMA-7B, and an encoder-decoder model, FLAN-T5-XXL. Reported results include up to 26-fold prompt compression, up to 40% fewer floating-point operations, 4.2% wall-time speedups, and storage savings with minimal output-quality loss. The difference between arithmetic savings and elapsed-time savings also shows why the two efficiency measures should be interpreted separately.
neurips-2023-learning-to-compress-prompt.tldr: Gisting trains language models to cache compressed prompt tokens, reducing computation and storage with minimal reported quality loss.

paragraphs: A local explanation describes a black-box model's decision for a particular example. For that explanation to be useful, it should follow the model faithfully while remaining reasonably stable across nearby examples. This paper proposes a model-agnostic explanation method inspired by invariant risk minimization, adapting that principle to local explanations with consistent directions of feature influence.

The method uses a game-theoretic formulation. Its analysis shows a strong tendency to remove features whose black-box gradients abruptly change sign nearby. In other situations, it assigns more conservative feature attributions. These behaviors matter for recourse because an explanation suggesting a direction of change becomes harder to act on when that direction reverses around the example.

Experiments on tabular, image, and text data report better explanations than LIME using neighborhoods built from random perturbations. In some cases, results are comparable to methods that use realistic neighbors sampled from the data manifold. The approach is described as simple and efficient to train, and it identifies locally stable features without requiring side information such as a partial causal graph.
neurips-2023-locally-invariant-explanati.tldr: A local invariant-learning method produces more stable explanations by discouraging feature attributions whose directions change abruptly nearby.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning improves a policy using an existing dataset. A major difficulty arises when learning considers actions outside that dataset's distribution: unreliable value estimates can push the policy in the wrong direction. MISA addresses this by using mutual information between dataset states and actions to constrain the direction of policy improvement.

The framework builds lower bounds on mutual information using the policy and its Q-values. The authors show that optimizing the bound is equivalent to maximizing, on the offline data, the likelihood of a policy improved by one step. This connects the learning objective to keeping policy improvement within the data manifold. Mutual-information regularization is applied to both policy evaluation and policy improvement.

MISA also places conservative Q-learning and behavior-regularization methods within a common framework as special cases. Across three proposed variants, experiments find that tighter mutual-information bounds correspond to better offline learning performance. Evaluations on D4RL report significant gains over a wide range of baselines, including 742.9 total points on gym-locomotion tasks. The tighter-bound relationship is an empirical finding from these evaluations.
neurips-2023-mutual-information-regulari.tldr: MISA uses mutual-information bounds to keep offline policy improvement aligned with recorded data and improves reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Outdoor lighting can substantially change how a street scene looks, creating difficulties for robot perception systems trained under different conditions. LightSim addresses this by generating controllable camera data under varied illumination. Its purpose is to expand the lighting conditions available for training through realistic simulation built from collected sensor data.

The system automatically constructs lighting-aware digital twins, separating moving actors from the static background while representing geometry, appearance, and estimated lighting. These scene representations support inserting, modifying, and removing actors, as well as rendering new viewpoints. LightSim combines physically based rendering with learnable deferred rendering to relight the edited scenes.

Controllable changes include moving the sun, adjusting its brightness, and modifying the resulting shadows. The system produces camera videos intended to remain consistent across space and time, so lighting changes operate across a scene and sequence rather than as isolated image edits. Experiments report more realistic relighting than prior work and show that training perception models with LightSim-generated data can significantly improve their performance.
neurips-2023-neural-lighting-simulation-.tldr: LightSim builds editable urban digital twins and realistically relights them to generate training videos that can improve robot perception.

paragraphs: Geodesic queries ask for distances and paths along a shape's surface. Many geometry-processing applications need large numbers of these queries between arbitrary points, which can make traditional mesh algorithms costly. NeuroGF investigates whether a learned neural representation can store this information in a form that supports efficient distance and path queries.

The proposed neural geodesic field learns an implicit representation of all-pairs geodesics for a given 3D mesh. Once learned, it can answer queries between arbitrary points on that model. The framework also offers a unified representation for both the underlying 3D geometry and its geodesics, connecting the shape description with information about travel along its surface.

Evaluations on common object models and meshes of captured scenes report strong representation accuracy and query efficiency. The authors further extend the initial approach, which fits an individual model, into generalizable learning frameworks. These accept input formats including unstructured point clouds and show satisfactory performance on unseen shapes and categories. This extension broadens the approach beyond separately learning every queried mesh.
neurips-2023-neurogf-a-neural-representa.tldr: NeuroGF learns neural representations of surface distances and paths for efficient geodesic queries on 3D shapes.

paragraphs: Homomorphic encryption lets graph convolutional networks process encrypted graph data in the cloud, but its computation and memory costs can be substantial. The paper observes that generic encrypted matrix-multiplication methods miss useful structure in how graph layers aggregate node features. Penguin reorganizes encrypted data to take advantage of that particular computation pattern.

Its packing scheme operates across the two dimensions of node-feature data, combining graph-node partitioning with feature interleaving. After feature reduction, an interleaved assembly step uses empty ciphertext slots to merge ciphertexts. This reduces costly rotation operations and makes more effective use of the encrypted representation as the network changes the feature dimensions.

Theoretical analysis and experiments with popular graph models and datasets support the efficiency gains. Reported improvements reach approximately tenfold speedup and around 79% lower computational memory overhead relative to state-of-the-art solutions. These figures describe the reported results rather than a uniform guarantee for every workload. The authors also identify protection of both graph structure and features during accelerated encrypted inference as a distinguishing contribution.
neurips-2023-penguin-parallel-packed-hom.tldr: Penguin packs encrypted graph features around GCN computation patterns, achieving reported speedups of up to roughly tenfold.

paragraphs: Many policy-based reinforcement learning algorithms alternate between estimating a policy's value and improving that policy. Both steps are usually approximate. This paper studies how those approximation errors affect performance when the goal is average reward, a setting where the relevant objective is sustained reward rather than a discounted total.

A common approach uses a discount factor close to one to approximate a long horizon. However, existing error bounds grow with the square of that horizon. Dividing by the horizon to obtain an average does not solve the problem: the resulting bounds still diverge as the horizon grows. They therefore fail to provide meaningful control of average-reward performance through that limiting argument.

The authors derive nontrivial finite-time error bounds directly for average-reward Markov decision processes. These bounds approach zero as the policy-evaluation and policy-improvement errors approach zero. This supplies a theoretical connection between the accuracy of the two approximate steps and the resulting policy's performance. The contribution is a performance analysis for approximate policy iteration and related algorithms, addressing the failure of the discounted-bound approach.
neurips-2023-performance-bounds-for-poli.tldr: The paper derives finite-time average-reward performance bounds that vanish as policy-evaluation and policy-improvement errors vanish.

paragraphs: Novelty detection aims to identify inputs that fall outside the distribution a model knows. Diffusion-based detectors often use reconstruction behavior, but they can struggle when an abnormal image shares background information with familiar images. In that situation, background similarity can obscure a meaningful difference in what the image depicts.

Projection Regret builds on the observation that a diffusion model can project an image toward an in-distribution image with similar background information. The method measures the perceptual distance between the original image and that projection. Because background content can dominate even this distance, it compares the measurement against recursive projections to cancel background bias.

The key idea is to judge the first projection in relation to further projections rather than using its perceptual distance alone. This comparison is designed to reduce the influence of nonsemantic information on the abnormality score. Extensive experiments report a significant improvement over prior generative-model-based novelty detectors. The findings support the proposed comparison as an effective way to address background bias within the evaluated detection setting.
neurips-2023-projection-regret-reducing-.tldr: Projection Regret compares recursive diffusion projections to reduce background bias and improve novelty detection.

paragraphs: Real noisy images can differ from synthetic training noise, while collecting matching clean images is expensive. Self-supervised denoising instead learns from noisy images themselves. To prevent simple copying in the approach discussed here, an output pixel must not depend on its corresponding input pixel, a property called J-invariance.

Blind-spot networks enforce that separation, but adding operations such as downsampling can accidentally expose the hidden pixel. This restricts architectural choices and the information a denoiser can gather safely. PUCA proposes a J-invariant U-Net architecture that uses patch-unshuffle and patch-shuffle operations to greatly expand receptive fields while preserving the required separation between corresponding input and output pixels.

The model also uses dilated attention blocks to incorporate global context. Together, these components address how to give the network broader image information without undermining the self-supervised training constraint. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance over existing self-supervised denoising methods. The contribution therefore combines an architectural solution to information leakage with empirical evidence that broader context improves denoising in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2023-puca-patch-unshuffle-and-ch.tldr: PUCA expands image context while preserving blind spots, improving reported self-supervised denoising performance.

paragraphs: Epistemic uncertainty concerns uncertainty associated with the predictive model. In the formulation studied here, estimating it requires integrating a product: how plausible a model is under the posterior and how much its predictions diverge from a reference. The paper argues that methods focused primarily on posterior sampling can inadequately estimate this combined quantity.

QUAM searches for regions where the full product is large. The resulting adversarial models have both high posterior support and substantial predictive disagreement with the reference model. The word adversarial refers to alternative models, rather than altered input examples. Their role is to expose plausible disagreement that contributes strongly to the uncertainty integral.

By targeting the quantity actually being integrated, QUAM achieves lower approximation error than the previous approaches discussed in the paper. Vision experiments report stronger epistemic uncertainty estimation and better performance on challenging tasks. The central contribution is a change in how models are sought for uncertainty estimation: predictive disagreement participates directly in the search alongside posterior plausibility.
neurips-2023-quantification-of-uncertain.tldr: QUAM estimates epistemic uncertainty by seeking plausible models that also strongly disagree with a reference model.

paragraphs: The Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, or HSIC, measures dependence between random vectors and supports tests of statistical independence. Although it can measure nonlinear relationships, its behavior can change when the vectors contain many dimensions. This paper studies dimensions growing at different rates, connecting settings between fixed-dimensional and very-high-dimensional analyses.

The authors establish that, under the independence null hypothesis in their analysis, a rescaled HSIC statistic converges to a standard normal distribution. They also give a general condition under which HSIC-based tests retain nontrivial power, meaning an ability to detect dependence. Decomposing that condition reveals how increasing dimension changes sensitivity to nonlinear relationships.

The resulting picture depends jointly on sample size, vector dimensions, and dependence among coordinates within each vector. Different combinations allow HSIC to capture different kinds of association between the vectors. Numerical studies validate the theoretical findings. The paper thus explains why calling HSIC a nonlinear dependence measure does not, by itself, describe which relationships it will detect effectively in a particular high-dimensional setting.
neurips-2023-statistical-insights-into-h.tldr: The paper characterizes how dimension, sample size, and internal dependence affect HSIC's ability to detect statistical relationships.

paragraphs: With N units and p interventions, predicting each unit's outcome under every intervention combination involves N times 2^p causal quantities. Observing every case quickly becomes infeasible. Observational data add another difficulty: which combinations are observed can be related to the outcomes that would occur, creating confounding.

Synthetic Combinations uses structure across both units and intervention combinations. It assumes the potential-outcome matrix is approximately rank r, capturing latent similarities among units. It also assumes an approximately s-sparse Fourier representation, restricting the complexity of interactions among interventions. Under this model, the authors establish identification despite unobserved confounding and provide an estimation procedure with finite-sample consistency under precise observation-pattern conditions.

The stated observation requirement scales as a polynomial in r multiplied by N plus s squared times p. This improves on the stated scaling of methods that exploit structure along only one of the two axes. The result matters because it replaces exhaustive observation of exponentially many combinations with a structured estimation problem. Its guarantees depend on the model's similarity, sparsity, and observation conditions.
neurips-2023-synthetic-combinations-a-ca.tldr: Synthetic Combinations estimates personalized intervention-combination outcomes efficiently under joint low-rank, sparsity, and observation-pattern conditions.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning relies on experience from training tasks to learn a new task from very few labeled examples. Its motivation assumes those tasks are related, but that leaves two questions: how to measure the relationship and how it affects adaptation. This paper addresses both through task attributes.

The authors propose Task Attribute Distance, or TAD, as a model-independent measure of task relatedness. Because the metric does not depend on a particular few-shot model, it can support analysis across different methods. They derive a generalization-error bound for a novel task that establishes a theoretical connection between this attribute-based distance and the difficulty of adapting to that task.

Experiments on three benchmarks support TAD as a measure of relatedness and adaptation difficulty across several few-shot methods. The reported usefulness also extends to cases where models do not explicitly learn attributes or human-annotated attributes are unavailable. The contribution offers a shared way to characterize task relationships and study their consequences, rather than treating relatedness only as an informal explanation for successful transfer.
neurips-2023-understanding-few-shot-lear.tldr: Task Attribute Distance provides a model-independent measure linking task relatedness to few-shot adaptation difficulty.

paragraphs: User-level differential privacy protects a person's contribution across their examples. Earlier generic learning approaches focused on settings where each person had enough examples to solve the learning problem individually. This paper instead studies the example-scarce setting, where each user contributes only a few examples and learning must make effective use of information across users.

For approximate differential privacy, the authors provide a generic transformation from an item-level private algorithm to a user-level private algorithm. Roughly, with m examples per user, the result yields a square-root-of-m multiplicative saving in the required number of users for the same utility, with dependence on privacy parameters. It recovers most known problem-specific bounds and supplies new ones, including for PAC learning.

For pure differential privacy, the paper adapts the exponential mechanism to the user-level setting. This produces new bounds for private PAC learning, hypothesis selection, and distribution learning. Some of these bounds are shown to be near-optimal. Together, the results establish generic approaches for obtaining useful user-level protection even when individual users have limited data.
neurips-2023-user-level-differential-pri.tldr: The paper develops generic user-level private learning methods for settings where each user contributes only a few examples.

paragraphs: This paper develops an energy-based probabilistic framework for particle-physics events at the Large Hadron Collider. Energy-based models offer flexibility in the form of the function used to represent a distribution. The authors use that flexibility to build a model intended to serve several physics tasks within a common probabilistic approach.

The framework describes higher-order interactions among particles, allowing its representation of an event to account for relationships involving multiple particles. It supports different encoding architectures and uses implicit generation. These design choices give the approach flexibility in how events are represented while retaining a generative foundation for the different applications.

The proposed uses include a parameterized event generator for physics simulation, an anomalous-signal detector described as free from spurious correlations, and an augmented event classifier for particle identification. The significance is the range of roles available to the same modeling framework: generating events, identifying unusual signals, and classifying particles. The abstract presents these as supported applications, without attaching numerical performance comparisons to those capabilities.
neurips-2023-versatile-energy-based-prob.tldr: An energy-based framework models particle interactions to support event generation, anomaly detection, and particle identification.
